title: Spring: filters, interceptors, AOP and async
description: Servlet filters, HandlerInterceptor callbacks, Spring AOP and its proxy limits, thread-per-request capacity, SseEmitter, @Async and WebFlux basics.
source: Spring Framework AOP and MVC documentation; Servlet specification; Spring Boot reference (embedded Tomcat defaults); Project Reactor documentation; Baeldung
seriesDescription: Spring Boot structure and DI, REST and validation, error handling, filters, async, API design, jobs and health. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.

questions.prompt: Match each Spring mechanism with the job it is best suited for.

right.text: Wrap the raw request/response before `DispatcherServlet`, e.g. token parsing or request-id logging
Use the resolved handler method in `preHandle/postHandle`, e.g. per-controller auth checks
Time or audit calls to service-bean methods, even outside HTTP
Translate exceptions from any controller into a uniform error body

questions.explanation: Filters are Servlet-container level, interceptors are Spring MVC level (they know the handler), aspects are proxy-based and work on any Spring bean, and advice classes handle exceptions.

questions.text: {1} runs before the handler and can stop the chain by returning false; {2} runs after the handler but before the view is rendered; {3} runs after the request completes, even when the handler threw.
questions.explanation: `doFilter` belongs to Servlet filters and `afterReturning` to AOP advice. `postHandle` is skipped when the handler throws, `afterCompletion` is not.

questions.prompt: Write a Spring aspect class `TimingAspect` (a bean) with an `@Around` advice that times every method of classes in package `com.acme.service` and its sub-packages, then returns the real result.

checks.label: uses @Around with an execution pointcut on com.acme.service
calls proceed() and returns its result
measures time with nanoTime or currentTimeMillis

questions.explanation: Forgetting `proceed()` silently swallows the call. Needs `spring-boot-starter-aop` in Boot 3 (renamed `spring-boot-starter-aspectj` in Boot 4). Pointcuts using `within()` or an annotation are valid alternatives.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Spring AOP advice does not run when a bean calls one of its own advised methods via `this`.
questions.reason: Spring AOP is proxy-based, and an internal call bypasses the proxy.

whys.a: Correct: the call never leaves the target object, so the proxy that applies advice is skipped.

questions.explanation: Same root cause as `@Transactional` self-invocation. Fixes: refactor into another bean, call through the injected proxy of the bean itself, or use AspectJ weaving.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A Servlet filter that never calls `chain.doFilter(request, response)` stops the request from reaching the controller.
questions.reason: Filters can be ordered with `@Order` or a `FilterRegistrationBean`.

whys.a: Wrong: ordering does not explain why the request stops.
whys.b: Correct: both true; the chain simply is not continued, and ordering is an unrelated fact.
whys.d: Wrong: A is true; a filter can also short-circuit with its own response.

questions.explanation: Auth filters use exactly this to return 401 early. Order matters: a security filter must run before a logging filter that reads the principal.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: `HandlerInterceptor.postHandle` is called even when the controller method throws an exception.
questions.reason: `afterCompletion` is called after the handler finishes, including when it threw (provided `preHandle` returned true).

whys.d: Correct: postHandle is skipped on exceptions; afterCompletion is the callback for cleanup.

questions.explanation: Put resource cleanup and metrics in `afterCompletion`, not `postHandle`.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which statements about Spring async and WebFlux are correct?

options.text: `@Async` only takes effect when `@EnableAsync` is present and the call goes through the proxy.
options.why: Without both, the method runs synchronously on the caller's thread.
Those are the supported return types; callers get the result through the future.
That is the core of Reactor's model.

options.text: A `Mono` does the work as soon as the method returns it, without subscription.
options.why: Reactive streams are lazy; nothing happens until subscribed (WebFlux subscribes for you).

options.text: An exception thrown in a `void` `@Async` method propagates to the caller.
options.why: It does not; it goes to an `AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler`.
Proxy-based advice cannot intercept private methods.

questions.explanation: WebFlux needs a non-blocking stack end to end; one blocking JDBC call on an event-loop thread stalls every request that thread serves. Virtual threads (Java 21) are the simple alternative.

questions.prompt: Write a Spring filter class `RequestIdFilter` that extends `OncePerRequestFilter`, sets the response header `X-Request-Id` to a random UUID string, and then continues the filter chain.
questions.explanation: `OncePerRequestFilter` guarantees one execution per request even with forwards and error dispatches. Forgetting `chain.doFilter` silently stops the request. Put the id into the logging `MDC` as well so every log line carries it.

questions.prompt: Write a Spring MVC `GET /events` handler named `events` that returns an `SseEmitter`, produces `text/event-stream`, sends the text `"tick"` to the client with `send(...)` and then completes the emitter.
questions.explanation: In real code the emitter is handed to another thread or a registry that keeps sending `events`; remove it on completion, timeout and error callbacks. A `Flux<ServerSentEvent<String>>` with WebFlux is the reactive alternative.

questions.prompt: A Spring Boot MVC application runs on embedded Tomcat with the default maximum of 200 request threads. Every request blocks its thread for 1 second, and 600 requests arrive at the same instant. About how many seconds until the last one finishes?
questions.explanation: Tomcat serves 200 requests at a time, so 600 requests need 3 rounds of 1 s: about 3 s. The thread-per-request model is why slow downstream calls exhaust the pool; virtual threads or non-blocking I/O change the arithmetic.

questions.prompt: Interceptors A, B and C are registered in that order with `registry.addInterceptor(...)`. Every `preHandle` returns true and the handler succeeds. At which position (1 = first) does `A's afterCompletion` run?
questions.explanation: `preHandle` runs in registration order A, B, C, while `postHandle` and `afterCompletion` run in reverse: C, B, A. So `A's afterCompletion` is third, like the unwinding of nested `try/finally` blocks.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A Servlet Filter registered as a Spring bean in Spring Boot applies to every request path by default.
questions.reason: Filters run after `DispatcherServlet` has chosen the controller method.

whys.a: Wrong: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (the default URL pattern is /*); R is false because filters run before DispatcherServlet and know nothing about the handler.

questions.explanation: Restrict a filter with a `FilterRegistrationBean` URL pattern, or choose a `HandlerInterceptor` when you need the resolved handler.

questions.prompt: You need a check that depends on an annotation present on the controller method that is about to run. Which mechanism sees that handler method?

options.text: A Servlet Filter, which runs before routing and sees only the raw request.
options.why: Filters cannot see which controller method will handle the request.

options.text: A `@ControllerAdvice` class, because it wraps every controller.
options.why: Advice handles exceptions and binding, not pre-handler checks.

options.text: An `@Around` aspect on the service layer that sits below the controller.
options.why: It runs below the controller, too late to stop the web request early.
Correct: interceptors run after handler mapping, so they know the target.

questions.explanation: Use a filter for container-level concerns, an interceptor for MVC-aware checks, and an aspect for non-web service logic.

questions.prompt: True or false: a Servlet filter can wrap the request in a caching wrapper (such as `ContentCachingRequestWrapper`) so the body can be read again later in the chain.

options.why: Correct: filters may pass substituted request and response objects down the chain.
Wrong: the chain accepts any `ServletRequest` implementation, so wrapping is allowed.

questions.explanation: This is how request logging and signature checks read a body twice. A `HandlerInterceptor`, in contrast, cannot replace the request object.

questions.prompt: True or false: a `HandlerInterceptor` can replace the `HttpServletRequest` object that the controller method will receive.

options.why: Wrong: `preHandle` only receives the request; it has no way to hand a different one onward.
Correct: interceptors can read, mutate attributes or stop the chain, but not substitute the request object.

questions.explanation: Request substitution is a Servlet filter capability, one more reason to choose a filter for body caching or decompression.
